Polymeric nanotherapeutics improve solubility and pharmacokinetics of therapeutic cargoes through controlled drug delivery.
PEGylation of polymeric nanoparticles provides a hydration layer and steric barrier that reduces serum protein binding and clearance by the mononuclear phagocytic system.
Genexol-PM is a PEG–PLA micellar formulation of paclitaxel approved in South Korea for metastatic cancer treatment.
CRLX101 is a cyclodextrin–PEG copolymer conjugated with camptothecin, forming nanoparticles of 20–60 nm with a circulation half-life of ~1 day in rodents.
CALAA-01 is a transferrin-targeted PEG–cyclodextrin nanoparticle delivering siRNA, currently in Phase Ib clinical trials for melanoma.
BIND-014 is a PEG–PLGA nanoparticle loaded with docetaxel and targeting PSMA, showing increased tumor drug concentration and reduced toxicity in preclinical models.
PEG molecular weight of 5000 Da and high surface density favor brush-like conformations that enhance stealth properties.
Repeated administration of PEGylated nanoparticles can induce anti-PEG IgM antibodies, causing accelerated blood clearance.
HPMA polymers allow multiple drug conjugations and form unimolecular micelles with improved pharmacokinetics.
Zwitterionic polymers like poly(carboxybetaine) provide stronger hydration via electrostatic interactions, reducing protein adsorption more effectively than PEG.
Polysaccharides such as heparin and dextran prolong nanoparticle circulation by mimicking the glycocalyx and reducing immune clearance.
Incorporation of ganglioside GM1 into liposomes increases blood circulation time by mimicking erythrocyte surface carbohydrates.
Poly(amino acid)s such as polyglutamic acid reduce phagocytic uptake via electrostatic repulsion and are biodegradable.
Nanoparticles can exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect for passive tumor targeting.
Clinical trials of polymeric nanotherapeutics show prolonged systemic circulation, sustained drug release, and improved tumor accumulation compared to free drugs.
PEG alternatives are being explored due to immunogenicity concerns, including HPMA, zwitterionic polymers, and polysaccharides.
Nanoparticle formulations in clinical trials include SP1049C, CRLX101, NC-6004, NK105, NK911, NK012, BIND-014, CALAA-01, and Genexol-PM.
The accelerated blood clearance phenomenon is linked to anti-PEG antibody production and complement activation.
Polymeric nanoparticles can be functionalized with targeting ligands to improve cellular uptake and therapeutic efficacy.
Biologically inspired stealth strategies mimic natural cell surface features to evade immune clearance.
